title: FSSAI Crackdown on Misleading Food Labels Hits Dabur, Marico, Ferrero and More
excerpt: India's food safety regulator has issued notices to dozens of companies over misleading '100%' claims, fake organic labels, and unsubstantiated health claims, forcing brands from Dabur to MasterChow to overhaul their packaging.
body:
• FSSAI has issued notices to dozens of food companies since June 2026, targeting misleading claims like '100% Natural,' 'Heart Pro,' and fake organic certifications.
  • Dabur was ordered to halt sales of honey, coconut oil, ghee, and other products carrying unverifiable '100%' claims. Its shares fell 4% following the action.
  • Six energy drink brands including Red Bull, Sting, and Monster Energy received notices for using the term 'energy drink' — a category that does not officially exist under Indian food regulations.
  • Compliance demand has surged, with label review requests jumping 40% at testing labs and over 50 brands signing up with AI-driven compliance platforms.

A Sweeping Regulatory Push

India's Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI) has launched its most aggressive crackdown on misleading food labels in years, issuing notices to dozens of companies across categories — from honey and cooking oil to chocolate, noodles, and energy drinks.

The regulator has not introduced any new laws. Instead, it has ramped up enforcement of the existing Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the FSS (Advertising & Claims) Regulations, 2018, with a far more public approach — naming companies on social media and inviting consumers to report misleading packaging through its Food Safety Connect mobile app.

The heightened scrutiny follows months of criticism from health influencers and NGOs on social media, who argued that India's food labelling standards lag behind those in Europe.

Dabur Ordered to Stop Sales

The highest-profile action came on August 3, when FSSAI barred Dabur India from selling food products carrying "100%" claims — including honey, apple cider vinegar, virgin coconut oil, sesame oil, cow ghee, coconut water, and coconut milk.

The regulator flagged claims like "100% Natural," "100% Pure," and "100% Purity Guaranteed" as "ambiguous, unverifiable and likely to mislead consumers." It also found that Dabur's organic apple cider vinegar and organic honey displayed the Jaivik Bharat logo without a valid FSSAI organic endorsement.

"Dabur stands by the purity and quality of its products and has never made any misleading claims. However, as a good corporate citizen, Dabur had already initiated transitioning of the product labels."

— Dabur India, in a statement

Dabur's shares fell nearly 4% the day after the order — their steepest drop in 20 weeks. The company said most affected labels and advertisements have either already been revised or are in the process of transition, and that it is seeking legal advice.

Brands Across Categories Under Fire

The crackdown has been broad. In June, FSSAI issued notices to brands including Emami's Healthy & Tasty cooking oil, Neuherbs True Vitamin, The Health Factory, and Troovy for using trade names that "appear to be in contravention of applicable FSSAI regulations." Organic brands Organic Wisdom, Shine Organic, and Two Brothers Organic Farms were flagged for claiming organic status without the required certifications.

A second wave targeted Marico's Saffola Heart Pro cooking oil for using heart imagery and claims like "Good Fats Balance" without scientific substantiation. Ferrero's Kinder Joy was flagged for claiming to be "rich in milk solids" when its ingredient composition did not support the claim. MasterChow's ramen noodles were called out for "100% Natural" and "Freshly Made" claims.

In July, six energy drink brands — Red Bull, PepsiCo's Sting and Adrenaline Rush, Reliance's Campa Energy, Hell Energy, and Coca-Cola-backed Monster Energy — received notices for using the term "energy drink" on packaging. FSSAI pointed out that no such category officially exists under Indian food safety regulations.

Industry Scrambles to Comply

The enforcement wave has triggered a rush among food companies to review and revise their packaging. In May, clean-label brand The Whole Truth preemptively dropped its "no added sugar" claim, replacing it with "sweetened with dates" after receiving a show-cause notice prompted by a rival's complaint.

Testing and compliance firms have seen a sharp uptick in business. Equinox Labs reported a 40% jump in label review requests in the three months following the crackdown. Over 50 brands signed up with BettrLabs, an AI-driven compliance platform, in a single month to validate their product portfolios against FSSAI norms.

"A year ago, most requests were transactional. Brands would send us a product for testing and we'd return a report. Today, many of them come to us before a product is launched."

— Ashwin Bhadri, Founder and CEO of Equinox Labs

Larger companies are now auditing entire product portfolios rather than just the items under scrutiny, assuming that if one claim is questioned, similar claims across other products could follow.

What's Driving the Shift

The regulatory push comes amid rapid growth in India's health food market, valued at $25.8 billion in 2025 and projected to reach $59.8 billion by 2034, according to market research firm Imarc. Sales of protein bars, makhana, healthy chips, and nuts doubled to Rs 327.7 crore in the January–March 2026 quarter on quick commerce platforms alone.

As health-related claims have become a key competitive tool, the gap between marketing language and regulatory standards has widened — and FSSAI is now closing it. The regulator's actions have also extended beyond packaged food: in August, it seized 18,000 boxes of Diageo's whisky and vodka products over labelling violations, including misleading claims about maturation processes.

Diageo-owned United Spirits has challenged the FSSAI order in the Bombay High Court. The dispute underscores the broader tension: companies argue existing claims are industry-standard language, while the regulator insists they mislead consumers and violate the law.
nri_angle: The crackdown on misleading food labels in India is relevant to NRI consumers who purchase Indian food products abroad or during visits, and who rely on labelling claims when choosing imported Indian brands.
